Findings, stated in the abstract: markets populated by LLM agents show slower or no convergence toward equilibrium and deliver less efficient allocations than markets populated by humans; there is substantial heterogeneity both across model families and across market roles; and a lexical analysis of chain-of-thought traces finds the decision to execute a trade rather than keep incrementally adjusting price is associated with a shift from strategic language toward urgency. They publicly release the testing framework. Do not extrapolate to live venues — this is an experimental replication, not a study of real order flow, and the abstract gives no model names or sample sizes, so do not supply any. Pair it with Dutch Books for Language Models, already on the plate: that paper says LLM forecasts are incoherent as prices; this one says price discovery degrades when LLMs are the ones discovering. Together they are the empirical case to put in front of any agentic-commerce or AI-trading-agent pitch.
grafs: A paper announced in Thursday's arXiv listings takes the most-studied mechanism in experimental economics — the double auction — and swaps the human subjects for language models. Pawel Struski, Jakub Swistak, Inez Okulska and Przemyslaw Biecek replicate the seminal experiments with LLM agents as buyers and sellers and ask whether the mechanism still does its job. Their answer: markets populated by LLM agents show slower or no convergence toward equilibrium and deliver less efficient allocations than markets populated by humans.

The authors frame this as an alignment question of a kind that rarely gets tested — not whether a model is safe or truthful, but whether it is compatible with a market mechanism built for people. They find substantial heterogeneity both across model families and across market roles, so buyer-side and seller-side behavior are not symmetric. A lexical pass over the agents' chain-of-thought traces turns up one behavioral tell: the decision to execute a trade, rather than keep incrementally adjusting price, is associated with a shift from strategic language toward urgency.

Read it beside “Dutch Books for Language Models,” also on this plate. That paper prices LLM forecasts as bets and finds them incoherent; this one finds that when LLMs are the participants, price discovery itself degrades. Neither is a study of live order flow, and the abstract names no models and no sample sizes, so nobody should extrapolate to a venue. But the load-bearing assumption under every agentic-commerce and AI-trading-agent pitch is that these agents transact competently, and the experimental record is now pointing the other way. The testing framework is public.

stories.hed: Differentiable market clearing: siting a data center that moves its own power price
stories.dek: Treat market clearing as an autodiff layer and gradients flow from planning cost back through cleared prices. 50 MW across six buses, 36 operating states, worst-case gaps of 2.3% and 8.5%.
stories.action: arXiv 2609.02646, “Differentiable Electricity-Market Clearing for Gradient-Based Planning,” Luca Mungo, Maarten P. Scholl and Arnau Quera-Bofarull; submitted Sept. 2, 2026, cs.LG with cs.CY, announced in the Sept. 3 listings. The premise, in the authors' own words, is the quotable part: “Planning a large data center is difficult because a facility big enough to matter changes the electricity prices it will pay.” Method: market clearing is a constrained optimization solved anew in every operating condition, so simulating it tells a planner how a candidate plan performs but not how to improve it; the authors instead treat clearing as a differentiable optimization layer, where each forward pass solves the market and reverse-mode automatic differentiation propagates planning cost back through the cleared prices to the plan. They validate the gradients against finite differences. Experiment, and keep it exactly this size: allocating 50 MW of data-center load across six candidate buses in two synthetic networks, under a fixed cost per active site, evaluated over 36 operating states. Result: judged against exhaustive enumeration of all site combinations, gradient optimization recovers the continuous allocations almost exactly, with worst-case objective gaps of 2.3% and 8.5% of the cost difference between the best and worst single site. The disclosed failure mode is worth printing because it is honest: near the cost at which a site should close, the smooth relaxation shrinks the site instead of closing it, so discrete transitions arrive late. Be explicit that the networks are synthetic and the scale is small — this is a framing contribution, not a deployable siting tool. Why our reader cares: every AI-capex model in circulation treats the power price as exogenous. This one makes the load endogenous and hands you a gradient, which is the right way to underwrite hyperscaler siting and PPAs like Google–Fervo, and the right lens for utility and IPP equity work.
grafs: “Planning a large data center is difficult because a facility big enough to matter changes the electricity prices it will pay.” That sentence opens a paper announced in Thursday's arXiv listings by Luca Mungo, Maarten P. Scholl and Arnau Quera-Bofarull, and it is the assumption most AI-capex models quietly violate. Power price goes in as an exogenous input, when a multi-hundred-megawatt load is large enough to reset the market it buys from.

Their fix is mechanical. Market clearing is a constrained optimization problem solved fresh in every operating condition, so a simulation tells a planner how a candidate plan scores but not how to improve it. The authors instead treat clearing as a differentiable optimization layer: each forward pass solves the market, and reverse-mode automatic differentiation propagates planning cost back through the cleared prices to the plan itself. They validate the gradients against finite differences, then allocate 50 MW of data-center load across six candidate buses in two synthetic networks under a fixed cost per active site, evaluated over 36 operating states. Against exhaustive enumeration of every site combination, the gradient method recovers the continuous allocations almost exactly, with worst-case objective gaps of 2.3% and 8.5% of the spread between the best and worst single site.

The disclosed failure is instructive: near the cost at which a site should shut, the smooth relaxation of a discrete site count shrinks the site rather than closing it, so discrete transitions arrive late. The networks are synthetic and 50 MW is small next to the gigawatt numbers on this page. But the framing is what travels — make the load endogenous and siting becomes a problem gradients can search, which is the honest way to underwrite a hyperscaler's bus choice, a PPA like Google's Fervo contract, or an IPP's exposure to the load showing up next door.

stories.hed: Square-root impact is manipulable at every decay exponent
stories.dek: Nonlinearity before memory forces the impact law affine. Gatheral's open region collapses to the line δ=1, and calibrated exponent pairs all sit in the manipulable set.
stories.action: arXiv 2609.02447, “Price manipulation in nonlinear transient impact models: rigidity before memory and complete positivity after memory,” by Minhyeok Lee; submitted Sept. 2, 2026, q-fin.TR, announced in the Sept. 3 listings. This is a real result for anyone who runs execution models, so get the statement right. The paper classifies both orders of composing a nonlinearity with a memory kernel. If an arbitrary instantaneous law f acts on the trading rate BEFORE any nonzero integrable Volterra kernel, then requiring nonnegative cost on every finite piecewise-constant round trip forces f to be affine — and linear for every nonzero convolution kernel. Concretely: power-law impact sgn(x)|x|^δ with δ>0 combined with power-law decay t^−γ for 0<γ<1 admits manipulation if and only if δ≠1, so square-root impact is manipulable at every decay exponent, and the region left open by Gatheral's slow-rate two-block bound δ+γ≥1 collapses to the line δ=1. The mechanism is a zero-volume chattering pump read out by two thin baseline trades, which is why it applies to singular kernels where earlier rigidity theorems needed a kernel bounded at zero. The converse is the constructive part: if a monotone readout acts AFTER the kernel, safety for all inputs and readouts is equivalent to complete positivity of the kernel — and square-root impact after power-law memory is manipulation-free. The abstract's closing line is the takeaway: “Calibrated exponent pairs all lie in the manipulable set: absent friction, concavity has to enter after the memory, not before it.” Say plainly that this is a statement about the idealized frictionless model, not a claim that anyone is extracting money from real venues — the paper quantifies the friction, the two-block phase and the switching complexity behind the power-law case. Audience: TCA, optimal execution, agency algos and model risk.
grafs: Square-root price impact with power-law decay is the industry-standard execution-cost model. A paper in Thursday's arXiv q-fin listings, by Minhyeok Lee, shows that in its usual form it is manipulable at every decay exponent — and that the fix is a change of composition order, not of parameters.

The result classifies both ways of combining a nonlinearity with a memory kernel. If an instantaneous law acts on the trading rate before a nonzero integrable Volterra kernel, then demanding nonnegative cost on every finite piecewise-constant round trip forces that law to be affine, and linear for every nonzero convolution kernel. For the standard parameterization — impact sgn(x)|x|^δ with decay t^−γ, 0<γ<1 — manipulation exists if and only if δ differs from 1. That means the region Gatheral's slow-rate two-block bound δ+γ≥1 left open collapses to the single line δ=1, and the mechanism, a zero-volume chattering pump read out by two thin baseline trades, works even for singular kernels that earlier rigidity theorems could not touch.

The constructive half is the actionable part. If instead a monotone readout acts after the kernel, safety for all inputs and all readouts is exactly equivalent to complete positivity of the kernel — and square-root impact applied after power-law memory is manipulation-free. The abstract's closing line is the instruction: “Calibrated exponent pairs all lie in the manipulable set: absent friction, concavity has to enter after the memory, not before it.” This is a statement about an idealized frictionless model rather than a claim that anyone is pumping real venues; the paper explicitly quantifies the friction, the two-block phase and the switching complexity that stand in the way. For a TCA or optimal-execution desk it is still a pointed question about where the concavity sits in your own model.

stories.hed: Moonshot files confidentially for a Hong Kong IPO, sources say
stories.dek: Reuters: the Kimi developer is targeting $3B. TechNode cites a separate round at about a $50B pre-money. Company: no comment.
stories.action: Treat as UNCONFIRMED and label it that way. Sourcing: Reuters, Hong Kong dateline, published 3:08 p.m. Singapore / 3:08 a.m. ET Sept. 3, citing three people with knowledge of the matter; the $3B raise target comes from one of those people. The A1-application detail and the ~$50B pre-money figure come from TechNode relaying HK01 (Chinese), not from Reuters — attribute them separately and do not merge them into one sourcing line. Moonshot said it had no comment on the market report and no information to disclose, and it had called an August report of an imminent filing untrue. Do not print a listing date, a bank syndicate, a float size, or a post-money number — none is sourced. The frame worth writing: this is the second Chinese frontier-model developer story on our plate alongside the unconfirmed DeepSeek $74B mark, and a confidential HKEX filing is the first hard procedural step, not a deal.
grafs: Moonshot, the Chinese AI developer behind the Kimi chatbot, has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, Reuters reported on Sept. 3, citing three people with knowledge of the matter. One of those people said the company is targeting a raise of $3 billion. The report carried a Hong Kong dateline and moved at 3:08 p.m. Singapore time, 3:08 a.m. ET.

TechNode, relaying the Chinese outlet HK01, described the submission as a confidential A1 application to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange filed this week, and reported separately that Moonshot is seeking new funding at a pre-money valuation of about $50 billion in what could be its final private round before a listing. Moonshot said it had no comment on the market report and no information to disclose; in August the company had called an earlier report that it planned to file within the month untrue.

Nothing here is confirmed by the company or by an exchange filing that is public — a confidential A1 is by construction not visible on HKEX until the issuer chooses to post it. What it establishes is procedural: the listing process has formally started, and the AI IPO pipeline now runs from Anthropic's pitched $100 billion-plus offering through SB Energy's S-1 to a Hong Kong tape that already absorbed the Mech-Mind listing this week.

stories.hed: Global yields at multiyear highs, and AI debt is now in the queue
stories.dek: Bunds highest since 2011, JGBs above 3%, gilts at a post-2008 peak. Data-center issuers are described as price-insensitive.
stories.action: Package as the rates frame under everything else on the plate. Use only what the piece actually says: Germany's 10-year at its highest since 2011, Japan's holding above 3%, U.S. 10-year Treasuries at their highest since November 2023, and UK gilts at a post-2008 peak in recent days; the sell-off is attributed to heavy government issuance, an oil-price shock reviving inflation concerns, and expectations that central banks stay tighter for longer. Named quotes available: Robin Brooks (Brookings) on a medium-term trend lasting years; Natalia Lojevsky (CIFC) on scope for further rises and on equities eventually catching up; Masahiko Loo (State Street) naming France as the standout vulnerable developed-market sovereign and flagging commercial real estate, private-equity-backed companies, direct-lending portfolios and lower-quality software as most exposed; Larry Holzenthaler (Catalyst Funds) on AI debt issuers being 'fairly price insensitive'; Thomas Browne (Keeley Teton) on small-caps and floating-rate debt. Deutsche Bank's estimate is a breakeven, not a forecast: 10-year yields could reach roughly 5.5% over a year, or about 6.4% over two years, before capital loss outweighs coupon income on a nominal total-return basis. Japan's debt is more than 200% of GDP with debt service estimated above 25% of FY2026 government expenses. Do not imply CNBC forecast any specific yield.
grafs: CNBC published a piece at 12:17 a.m. ET Sept. 3 arguing the world is entering a higher-rate era, with global yields at multiyear highs: Germany's 10-year at its highest since 2011, Japan's holding above 3 percent, U.S. 10-year Treasuries at their highest since November 2023, and UK gilts at a post-2008 peak in recent days. The latest leg is attributed to heavy government issuance, an oil-price shock that reignited inflation concerns, and expectations that central banks stay tighter for longer.

The line that matters for this desk is who is competing for the money. Technology companies are issuing enormous amounts of debt to build data centers, putting them in direct competition with governments and other corporate borrowers. “You have an enormous amount of debt being issued to fund different AI projects, and the issuers of that debt are fairly price insensitive,” said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds. Masahiko Loo of State Street Investment Management named commercial real estate, private-equity-backed companies, direct-lending portfolios and lower-quality software businesses as the most exposed borrowers — “the most leveraged ones that are accustomed to free money.”

Sovereigns carry the other side. Loo singled out France among developed markets on fiscal slippage and electoral uncertainty; Japan, with government debt above 200 percent of GDP and debt service estimated at more than a quarter of FY2026 expenses, illustrates the sensitivity most starkly. Deutsche Bank frames the investor math as a breakeven rather than a forecast: 10-year Treasury yields could climb to roughly 5.5 percent over the next year, or about 6.4 percent over two years, before capital losses outweigh coupon income on a nominal total-return basis. Robin Brooks of Brookings called it “the continuation of a medium-term trend that’ll keep going for many years.”

stories.hed: Korean chip exports +209% to a record $46.65B, 47.5% of all goods
stories.dek: August total goods exports $98.25B. One strategist puts chips at nearly 80% of export growth. Autos fell 29.8%.

also.label: Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources (MOTIR)

stories.action: This is the cleanest single macro read-through on AI capex concentration we have had. Stick to the reported figures: semiconductor exports +209% year over year to a record $46.65 billion in August, 47.5% of the country's $98.25 billion in goods exports, per the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources, which attributed the surge mainly to AI infrastructure demand as large cloud providers including Google and Amazon expanded capital spending. Non-semiconductor exports climbed 20%; automobile exports fell 29.8%, which the trade ministry largely attributed to summer-holiday timing and partial strikes. Named analysts: Jeff Ng (SMBC) estimating chips at nearly 80% of August export growth and expecting positive but moderating growth over 12 months; Dave Chia (Moody's Analytics) on a gradual slowdown being manageable versus an abrupt stall, and on the windfall fading if domestic demand cannot take over; Homin Lee (Lombard Odier) on 2-3% real growth still being sustainable and declining to call it over-reliance. The Bank of Korea raised its base rate to 3% in August, a second consecutive hike. Published 9:11 p.m. ET Sept. 2. Do not extrapolate a Samsung or SK Hynix revenue number from this — the release is national trade data, not company results.
grafs: South Korea's semiconductor exports surged 209 percent from a year earlier to a record $46.65 billion in August, accounting for 47.5 percent of the country's $98.25 billion in goods exports, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources reported. The ministry attributed the surge mainly to AI infrastructure demand as large cloud providers including Google and Amazon expanded capital spending. CNBC published the piece at 9:11 p.m. ET Sept. 2.

“In my estimate, semiconductor exports accounted for nearly 80% of export growth in August,” said Jeff Ng, head of Asia macro strategy at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation. Non-semiconductor exports still climbed 20 percent, but automobile exports fell 29.8 percent year over year, a decline the trade ministry largely attributed to summer-holiday timing and partial strikes.

The concern is the concentration itself. “A gradual slowdown would be manageable. An abrupt stall is a different matter, because the economy already runs at two speeds, and the sectors that would need to take up the slack are the ones under pressure today,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody's Analytics, who warned the windfall fades if chip demand cools while policy is still tightening — the Bank of Korea raised its base rate to 3 percent in August, a second consecutive hike. Homin Lee of Lombard Odier argued South Korea could still sustain 2 to 3 percent annual real growth if semiconductor momentum faded while other cyclical sectors held, and declined to characterize the position as over-reliance.

stories.hed: Netley closes its tertiaries fund; strategy now about $1.2B
stories.dek: Final close at an extended hard cap, up from $315M at the September 2025 launch. It buys secondaries stakes in secondaries funds.
stories.action: Small headline number, real structural story — write it as the latter. Confirmed on Netley's own newsroom, dated Sept. 3, 2026, London: total committed, deployable capital of approximately $1.2 billion following the final close of its flagship tertiaries fund at an extended hard cap. Compare against the franchise launch on Sept. 11, 2025 with $315 million, which Netley described as the private equity industry's first pool of capital dedicated to buying secondaries stakes in secondaries funds. Netley's own January 2026 Private Equity International piece, by Caspar Berendsen, Álvaro Rosado and Robert Perry, estimates the tertiary market at around $20 billion today and frames tertiaries as structural rather than cyclical — LP-led liquidity for holders of secondary-fund interests without forcing GP-led restructurings. Note the fund-name wording carefully: Netley's own page says “flagship tertiaries fund”; do not print a fund vintage number unless you can source it. No LP names, no target return, no management-fee terms are disclosed — do not supply any. The hook for our reader: a strategy that quadrupled its committed capital inside twelve months is a liquidity-demand signal about the secondaries market, priced by people who have to underwrite it.
grafs: Netley Capital said on Sept. 3 that it has approximately $1.2 billion in total committed, deployable capital for its tertiaries strategy, following the final close of its flagship tertiaries fund at an extended hard cap. The London firm launched the franchise on Sept. 11, 2025 with $315 million, describing it then as the private equity industry's first pool of capital dedicated to buying secondaries stakes in secondaries funds.

Tertiaries are one layer further out than the secondaries market everyone already tracks: rather than buying an LP's interest in a buyout fund, a tertiary buyer takes an interest in a secondaries fund. Netley's own framing, published with Private Equity International in January by co-founders Caspar Berendsen, Álvaro Rosado and Robert Perry, is that this is structural rather than cyclical — the answer to how thirty years of secondary-market growth left long-term commitments to secondary funds illiquid. They put the addressable tertiary market at roughly $20 billion today.

The number to hold onto is not the fund size but the slope: committed capital roughly quadrupled in twelve months, into a strategy whose entire premise is that institutions want out of positions early. Set that next to a rates tape at multiyear highs and it reads as the same story from the other end — the cost of staying illiquid is rising, and someone is raising money to price it.

stories.hed: Dutch Books for Language Models: arbitrage as a label-free coherence test
stories.dek: Andrews (MIT/NBER) and Sarkar (Chicago) price LLM stock-return forecasts as bets. Irrelevant context raises incoherence by an order of magnitude.
stories.action: The most quotable finance-AI paper of the day, and the framing does the work: score a model's probabilities the way a market maker would. Method: elicit probabilities from LLMs over events built from stock returns, then solve a linear program for the largest profit an arbitrageur could guarantee betting against those stated probabilities — de Finetti's theorem says that profit is zero exactly when the forecasts are coherent. It needs no outcome labels, so it works on unresolved events. Scale: 100 stock-days, 15 models, 365,100 total elicitations; the workhorse is GPT-OSS-120B, chosen because it predates the Aug. 15–Dec. 23, 2025 sample window, limiting lookahead bias. Headline numbers: mean arbitrage profit 0.002067 per unit gross stake (95% CI 0.001471–0.002737) for the workhorse; profit of at least 1% of stake in 6 of 100 stock-days. Across models, arbitrage profit ranges about 100x (0.002067 for GPT-OSS-120B to 0.1994 for Mistral Small 3.2) while Brier scores span only 0.1966–0.2157 — Spearman rank correlation 0.9143, and 101 of 105 pairwise profit comparisons exclude zero versus 32 for Brier. The killer detail for a general reader: appending “I'm feeling really optimistic about this” or “My phone battery is at 70%, by the way” significantly raises incoherence, in some arms by an order of magnitude. Also worth the graf: asking the full 14-event panel in one query drives incoherence nearly to zero, which is why the authors argue this is a post-training problem, not a capability ceiling. Be precise that the “profits” are a measure of incoherence, not tradable returns — the authors say so explicitly.
grafs: Isaiah Andrews (MIT and NBER) and Suproteem Sarkar (University of Chicago) posted a paper that evaluates language-model forecasts the way a market maker would evaluate a set of quotes. Using a theorem due to de Finetti, they treat a model's stated probabilities as prices and solve a linear program for the largest profit an arbitrageur could guarantee by betting against them. That profit is zero exactly when the forecasts are coherent, and computing it requires no outcome labels at all — so coherence can be scored on events that have not resolved.

The test bed is stock returns: 100 stock-days, 15 models, 365,100 elicitations, with GPT-OSS-120B as the workhorse because its August 2025 release predates the sample window. Incoherence is common. The workhorse averaged 0.002067 of guaranteed profit per unit of gross stake, with at least 1 percent of stake available in 6 of 100 stock-days. Across the 15 models arbitrage profit spans roughly a hundredfold, from 0.002067 to 0.1994 for Mistral Small 3.2, while Brier scores span only 0.1966 to 0.2157 — the two rankings agree (Spearman 0.9143) but coherence separates models far more sharply than accuracy does, with 101 of 105 pairwise comparisons significant versus 32 on Brier.

The part that will get quoted: coherence collapses on irrelevant context. Appending a note from the requester — “I'm feeling really optimistic about this,” “My phone battery is at 70%, by the way” — significantly raises arbitrage profit, in some arms by an order of magnitude, and richer logical relationships between events raise it further. Yet asking all 14 events in a single query drives incoherence nearly to zero, which is why the authors read this as a post-training problem rather than a ceiling. They are careful that the “profits” measure incoherence and are not tradable returns; the relevance to anyone pricing model output as a probability is the point.

stories.hed: Backtest the factor, or backtest the researcher?
stories.dek: Stanford's Giesecke and co-authors argue no agentic factor-mining system re-runs its own discovery loop. Six systems, two US panels, no consistent winner.

also.label: Jensen, Kelly, Pedersen — “Is there a replication crisis in finance?” (Panel A source)

stories.action: The right frame is governance, not another leaderboard. Yingjian Pan (Stanford MS&E / Advanced Financial Technologies Lab), Xiaowei Ding (Nanjing University) and Kay Giesecke (Hasso Plattner Institute) name the paradigm Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing and make one central claim: every existing system backtests its OUTPUT — the factor or the trade — and none re-executes its own discovery loop at more than one historical decision date, so a lucky run and a well-calibrated gate are indistinguishable from the reported Sharpe alone. Their proposed fix is a rolling re-execution of the whole loop at a sequence of historical dates under point-in-time constraints. Concrete results worth printing: their SEADS system is scored against five re-implemented baselines (AlphaAgent, AlphaForge, RD-Agent(Q), QuantaAlpha, Beyond Prompting) at a matched 300-candidate budget on two US equity panels — the US ex-microcap subset of the JKP characteristics database, and a CRSP/Compustat panel of 87 primitive variables checked for novelty against Bryzgalova et al.'s 45-characteristic reference. No single metric ranks the six consistently: Beyond Prompting leads productivity on both panels (96.4/85.0 admits vs SEADS's 14.0/13.8) and performance on Panel A (0.41 vs SEADS's 0.25), while SEADS leads Panel B performance (0.16) and novelty on both (0.65/0.46). In the rolling comparison all five discovery systems clear a no-discovery floor (mean Sharpe 0.82–0.96 vs 0.62 for the raw ~400-characteristic panel alone), and SEADS's own static arm falls to 0.71 — most of its rolling advantage is re-proposing, not the initial library. Report the authors' own limitations: admits in the tens, out-of-sample windows of 59–71 months, 5 static and 3 rolling replicates, Sharpe gross of trading costs, and a soft backbone-leakage residual because every role runs on one current model (GPT-5.2) rather than a release-dated one. Note the honest self-criticism too — 14 of 15 replicates in their own Figure 3 show combining admitted factors does not preserve their average individual quality.
grafs: Yingjian Pan of Stanford's Advanced Financial Technologies Laboratory, Xiaowei Ding of Nanjing University and Kay Giesecke of the Hasso Plattner Institute posted a paper naming and auditing a paradigm they call Agentic Empirical Asset Pricing: systems in which LLM agents autonomously run the hypothesis, formalization and evaluation loop over asset-pricing data with no human in any of the three steps. Their complaint is methodological. Every such system, they write, is evaluated the way a human-discovered factor is — hold out a test window, backtest the factor, report the Sharpe — and none re-executes the discovery loop itself at more than one historical decision date. A gate that admits a small fraction of candidates might be well calibrated, might be leaking through a bug, or might have drawn a favorable window, and one run's reported Sharpe cannot tell the three apart.

Their proposed standard scores a discovered pool on productivity, performance and novelty jointly — arguing none is meaningful without the other two — and then re-runs the entire loop at a sequence of historical decision dates under point-in-time constraints. Applied at a matched 300-candidate budget to their own SEADS system and five re-implemented baselines across two US equity panels, no single metric ranks the six consistently: Beyond Prompting leads productivity on both panels (96.4 and 85.0 admissions against SEADS's 14.0 and 13.8) and performance on the JKP panel (0.41 to SEADS's 0.25), while SEADS leads performance on the CRSP/Compustat panel (0.16) and novelty on both (0.65 and 0.46, lower being more novel).

The rolling result is the one that matters for anyone buying this software. All five discovery systems clear a no-discovery floor by a wide margin — mean Sharpe of 0.82 to 0.96 against 0.62 for the raw roughly 400-characteristic panel refit alone — but SEADS's own static arm, identical starting library and never re-discovering, reaches only 0.71. Most of the advantage is the act of re-proposing, not the library it started with. The authors are unusually forthcoming about limits: admitted-factor counts in the tens, out-of-sample windows of 59 to 71 months, five static and three rolling replicates, Sharpe reported gross of trading costs, a soft backbone-leakage residual from running every agent role on one current model rather than a release-dated one, and their own finding that in 14 of 15 replicates, combining admitted factors did not preserve their average individual quality.

stories.hed: Databricks opens Genie Agent mode to APIs and to files in Unity Catalog
stories.dek: Multi-step research plans with citations, now callable over SSE. Agents can read PDFs and decks alongside governed tables, up to 10 volumes.
stories.action: Write this for the finance-org reader, not the data-platform reader. What actually shipped, per the Databricks post of Sept. 2 by Hanlin Sun and Sydney Sundell: Agent mode — the agentic reasoning loop that plans, runs multiple iterative queries and returns a report with findings, visualizations and citations — is now available for all Genie Agents, and is exposed through Agent mode APIs with responses streaming over Server-Sent Events, so it can be embedded in custom apps, chatbots, scheduled reports and internal tools, with conversation retrieval for programmatic monitoring. Genie Agents can now analyze files in Unity Catalog volumes — PDFs, documents, slide decks, images — alongside governed tables in one conversation; builders can attach up to 10 volumes, unstructured analysis runs in Agent mode, and it respects Unity Catalog permissions so users see only files they can access, with content search indexing for retrieval over large volumes. Genie Code helps build a baseline agent from a description, diagnose specific conversation failures or benchmark runs, and summarize question topics and feedback trends in production. Chats can now be shared, and shared conversations stay live. The Databricks post does not give GA-versus-preview labels for each capability beyond pointing at the docs — say “shipped” or “now available” as the post does, and do not assert GA. The CFO angle: the governed-permissions story is the reason this is interesting for close, audit and contract review, and the honest caveat is that Databricks' own example questions (comparing two SOWs, exit-survey themes) are marketing examples, not benchmarked results.
grafs: Databricks said on Sept. 2 that Agent mode — the multi-step reasoning loop behind Genie Agents — is now available for all Genie Agents and, more consequentially, is exposed through APIs. Rather than answering from a single query, Agent mode creates and refines a research plan, explores data across iterative queries, and returns a report with findings, visualizations and citations. The APIs stream responses over Server-Sent Events, support follow-ups within a conversation, and allow retrieval of conversations and messages for programmatic monitoring, so the loop can be embedded in custom applications, chatbots, scheduled reports and internal tools instead of living only in the Databricks UI.

The second change is the one a controller will notice: Genie Agents can now analyze files stored in Unity Catalog volumes — PDFs, documents, slide decks and images — alongside governed tables in a single conversation. Builders can attach up to 10 volumes per agent, the analysis runs in Agent mode, and it respects Unity Catalog permissions, so a user only sees files they already have access to; content search indexes large volumes for faster retrieval. Databricks' own examples are cross-type questions — churned customers by region plus the themes in their exit surveys, or a comparison of two statements of work.

Curation gets its own tooling. Genie Code can build a baseline agent from a description of its purpose, example questions and data sources, drawing on Unity Catalog metadata and prior queries against those tables; diagnose specific conversation failures or benchmark runs and propose context fixes; and, in production, summarize the top question topics and feedback trends to surface knowledge gaps. Chats can now be shared with teammates or with agent authors, and shared conversations stay current as new messages and analyses land. What is being sold here is governed reasoning over the structured and unstructured halves of a finance org's evidence in one place — the examples in the post are illustrative, not benchmarked.

stories.hed: ISM Services 55.4 in August; prices 72.6, employment 47.8
stories.dek: 26th straight month of expansion. Business activity 61.7, new orders 60.9. Initial claims 206,000 the same morning.
stories.action: Package as this morning’s macro print, off the ISM report itself (10:00 a.m. ET, Sept. 3) and the DOL claims release (8:30 a.m. ET). Stick to ISM’s own numbers: Services PMI 55.4% (+1.3 pts from July’s 54.1%), 26th consecutive month in expansion; Business Activity 61.7% (+2.6); New Orders 60.9% (+3.7); Employment 47.8% (+0.4, second straight month contracting); Supplier Deliveries 51.3% (−1.5, slower deliveries); Prices 72.6% (+2.3), above 70% for the fifth time in six months, 12-month average 68.5%, highest since April 2023; Inventories 56.7%; Backlog 55.6%; New Export Orders 56.3%; Imports 56.3%; twelve industries growing, five contracting. From DOL: initial claims 206,000 for the week ended Aug. 29 (+2,000; prior week revised to 204,000), 4-week average 207,250, continuing claims 1,779,000 for the week ended Aug. 22, insured unemployment rate 1.2%. Do not print a Fed-odds number unless you can source the futures print, and do not pre-write Friday’s payrolls.
grafs: The Institute for Supply Management said on Sept. 3 that its August Services PMI registered 55.4 percent, up 1.3 percentage points from July’s 54.1 percent and the 26th consecutive month of expansion in the services sector. Business Activity rose 2.6 points to 61.7 percent and New Orders rose 3.7 points to 60.9 percent, while the Employment Index contracted for a second straight month at 47.8 percent, a 0.4-point improvement from July’s 47.4 percent.

Price pressure is the part that matters for the rates desk. The Prices Index registered 72.6 percent, 2.3 points above July, above 70 percent for the fifth time in six months, with the 12-month average up to 68.5 percent — the highest since April 2023. Supplier Deliveries at 51.3 percent marked a 21st straight month of slower deliveries. Inventories jumped to 56.7 percent, Backlog of Orders to 55.6 percent, and both New Export Orders and Imports printed 56.3 percent. Twelve industries reported growth, five contraction.

Earlier the same morning the Labor Department reported 206,000 initial claims for the week ended Aug. 29, up 2,000 from a revised 204,000, with the four-week average at 207,250. Continuing claims were 1,779,000 for the week ended Aug. 22 and the insured unemployment rate held at 1.2 percent. Firm services activity with a hot prices index and a soft employment index is the awkward combination heading into Friday’s August payrolls report.

stories.hed: EQT closes $3.2B Coller Capital combination; Coller EQT launches
stories.dek: Base consideration paid in 80,360,882 shares (~7%); up to $500M contingent to March 2029. AUM €341B; secondaries becomes a fourth segment.

grafs: EQT AB said on Aug. 31 that it completed its combination with Coller Capital, which now operates as Coller EQT and is reported as a new Secondaries business segment alongside Private Capital, Infrastructure and Real Estate. The definitive agreement was announced on Jan. 22, 2026. EQT acquired 100 percent of the Coller Capital management company and the general partner entities controlling its funds, along with 10 percent of the carried interest in the most recent flagship, Coller International Partners IX.

Terms, per the release: base consideration of $3.2 billion on a cash- and debt-free basis, consisting of 80,360,882 newly issued EQT ordinary shares, about 7 percent of shares outstanding, with roughly $65 million of the base payable in cash at completion subject to customary purchase-price adjustments. Contingent consideration runs to $500 million based on Coller’s performance in the 12 months through March 2029; key Coller management receiving about 64 percent of that contingent amount have committed to reinvest net proceeds in EQT shares. EQT is entitled to invest in 35 percent of the carried interest in all future Coller closed-ended funds.

The combination lifts EQT’s total assets under management to €341 billion (€186 billion fee-generating) as of June 30, 2026, adds nine strategies across private equity and credit secondaries, and brings a combined evergreen platform above €10 billion in net asset value. Jeremy Coller was appointed Head and CIO of Coller EQT and joins EQT’s Executive Committee; CEO Per Franzén repeated the commitment to double Coller’s fee-generating AUM within four years. EQT cites Evercore’s H1 2026 secondary market review for first-half transaction volume above $120 billion, the strongest first half on record and up nearly 20 percent year on year.

stories.action: Third leg of the frontier-model week next to anthropic-fable and openai-astra, and the one with the clearest CFO angle. Stick to Google’s post: Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.8 Flash Cyber, third Flash release in six weeks; 3.8 Flash at the same introductory price as 3.7 Flash, $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, with the footnote that the introductory price expires Dec. 31, 2026 and list moves to $1.50 / $7.50 on Jan. 1, 2027 — that footnote is the story for anyone budgeting 2027 inference. Google says 3.8 Flash “works harder,” taking extra reasoning steps and calling tools iteratively, and may use more tokens at higher effort levels; 3.7 Flash stays supported for efficiency-first workloads. Benchmarks as printed: 54.9% on HLE-Verified, plus claimed leads on DeepSWE v1.1, Vals Finance Agent V2 and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark. For Cyber: frontier-level CyberGym performance, above 70% success on an internal 20-language vulnerability benchmark, CWE-Bench pass@1 of 47.2% versus 47.8% for a leading frontier model at lower cost, Chrome Security reporting 2.6x more correct patches than larger commercial models, Wiz reporting +7.5–9.7% recall at 2.3–5.2x lower cost. Access: consumers via AI Pro/Ultra, enterprises via Gemini Enterprise, developers via AI Studio / Antigravity; Cyber only through the Fairwind Program for governments, critical-infrastructure operators and software maintainers. The 86.2% CyberGym figure and the 650-member Fairwind count come from SiliconANGLE and The Verge, not the Google post — attribute them if used. Pair with fsb-bailey and hiddenlayer-b on the cyber-economics thread.
grafs: Google published Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber on Sept. 2, its third Flash release in six weeks and three weeks after 3.7 Flash. Both variants share the same foundational model; Google says the coding and reasoning gains came partly from training in cybersecurity, and that 3.8 Flash “works harder” on complex tasks, executing extra reasoning steps and calling tools iteratively, which can mean more tokens at higher effort levels. Developers who care more about token cost are told to use lower effort levels or stay on 3.7 Flash.

The pricing line is the one to file. Gemini 3.8 Flash launches at the same introductory price as 3.7 Flash, $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens — but the post’s footnote says the introductory price expires Dec. 31, 2026, and that from Jan. 1, 2027 the rate is $1.50 per million input and $7.50 per million output. That is a scheduled doubling of list price on a model whose own design choice is to spend more tokens. Google claims 54.9% on HLE-Verified and leads over 3.7 Flash and other frontier models on DeepSWE v1.1, Vals Finance Agent V2, and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark.

Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is not generally available: it reaches trusted defenders through the new Fairwind Program for government authorities, critical-infrastructure operators and software maintainers. Google reports frontier-level CyberGym performance, a success rate above 70% on an internal benchmark spanning 20 programming languages, and CWE-Bench pass@1 of 47.2% against 47.8% for a leading frontier model at significantly lower cost. Internally, the Chrome Security team is quoted producing 2.6 times more correct patches than much larger commercial models, Wiz reports 7.5–9.7% higher recall on its penetration-testing benchmark at 2.3–5.2 times lower cost, and Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research team says it found a critical foundational vulnerability in under two hours. SiliconANGLE puts the CyberGym score at 86.2%; The Verge puts Fairwind membership at 650, including CrowdStrike and the Center for Internet Security.

grafs: Félix, the Miami-based remittance company that runs inside WhatsApp, announced $200 million in new financing this week. Crunchbase News reports the structure as an $87 million Series C equity round led by Andreessen Horowitz, with QED Investors, Castle Island Ventures, Switch Ventures, Contour Venture Partners and Endeavor Catalyst participating, alongside a $113 million debt commitment from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund. FinSMEs describes the debt piece as a warehouse credit line. Total capital raised since the 2020 founding is close to $300 million.

Reported operating metrics: more than $8 billion in transactions processed to date, revenue up more than 2.5 times over the past year, and coverage from the United States into 11 Latin American markets including Mexico, Brazil, Costa Rica, Honduras and Peru. The company did not disclose a post-money valuation, saying only that it had increased threefold since the 2025 Series B, a $75 million round led by QED. Figures of roughly $1.4 billion appearing on aggregator sites are not company-confirmed.

The use of proceeds is the interesting part for anyone watching consumer fintech balance sheets: the equity funds engineering, AI and compliance, while the credit facility funds a lending book as Félix moves from pure remittances into savings, loans and top-ups delivered through third parties. Settlement runs on USDC and blockchain rails behind the WhatsApp conversation. It is the second equity-plus-facility raise on our finance plate in two days after TabaPay’s $155 million.

Same underlying model as Mythos 5.1; Fable is GA on API/AWS/GCP/Azure as claude-fable-5-1; Mythos is trusted-access only (Cyber Verification Program + Life Sciences Verification Program with US government). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) puts monitoring data in customer-controlled cloud; phased from this fall, with zero data retention for eligible customers until then. Do not invent IPO/valuation numbers. Keep Anthropic–Lambda $35B, Anthropic–MatX, and Anthropic S-1 on the open-watch ledger.
grafs: Anthropic on Sept. 1 introduced Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 as the same underlying model with different safeguard levels. Fable 5.1 is generally available today on the Claude API and through Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure under model id claude-fable-5-1. Mythos 5.1 is invitation-only through trusted access programs for vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences work; Anthropic says Mythos is currently limited to a set of U.S. organizations, with expansion coordinated with the U.S. government.

The enterprise print is the cache-read cut. Anthropic says Fable 5.1 list prices otherwise match Fable 5 — $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output — while cache reads now cost 75% less, or $0.25 per million tokens. The company estimates that change lowers cost by around 25% for typical workloads and by up to around 45% for highly agentic, context-heavy work. Pair that with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards: monitoring data stored in customer-controlled cloud infrastructure rather than on Anthropic’s systems, rolling out in phases beginning later this fall, with eligible customers able to use Fable 5.1 under zero data retention until EFS is available.

Anthropic’s own benchmarks (vendor-reported) put Fable 5.1 at 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 versus 42.0% for Fable 5 and 52.3% for Opus 5, with Mythos 5.1 at 60.9% under more permissive cyber safeguards; Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 at 52.6% versus 24.7% for Fable 5; CursorBench 3.2.0 at 73.4%. Separately, Anthropic says cyber safeguards for Fable now produce about 60% fewer interventions per Claude Code session than the prior Fable 5 setup, while still redirecting exploit generation and related dual-use cyber tasks. Keep this on the AI plate next to the existing Anthropic IPO banker story; do not treat Fable as confirmation of Lambda, MatX, or an S-1.

grafs: OpenAI on Sept. 1 said it now believes Astra meets the Critical cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework — the first model the company is designating at that level. In OpenAI’s words, with the right tools and access Astra can find previously unknown security flaws and develop ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step. The company says stronger safeguards were required during development and before release, and that after delaying parts of Astra’s development and release it believes those safeguards sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm for release under the Framework.

Access is gated. stories.hed: EU designates ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine
stories.dek: Commission IP/26/1772. OpenAI Ireland reports 159.1 million average monthly EU users. Extra DSA duties by January 2027.
stories.action: Package as an official DSA designation, not an OpenAI product launch and not a fine. Primary is IP/26/1772 (Brussels, 31 August 2026; footnote: updated on 01/09/2026). ChatGPT is designated a Very Large Online Search Engine because it is a hybrid AI system that can search the web. Reddit and Roblox are designated VLOPs the same day. User counts come from the Commission register (updated 31 August 2026), as reported by the provider: ChatGPT 159.1 million average monthly active users, Reddit 57.2 million, Roblox 46.6 million. Do not write “first AI system ever designated” — the Commission does not say that. Do not invent a fine, a user-count methodology fight, or a compliance cost. Four-month clock to extra VLOP/VLOSE duties, i.e. by January 2027. Commission supervises with Coimisiún na Meán for ChatGPT. PR: Commission has now designated 28 VLOPs and VLOSEs.
grafs: The European Commission designated ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine under the Digital Services Act on Aug. 31, and designated Reddit and Roblox Very Large Online Platforms the same day (IP/26/1772; the release was updated Sept. 1). The services declared that they reach at least 45 million average monthly users in the EU, the designation threshold. ChatGPT, the Commission said, is an AI system that can engage with users’ prompts “including by searching the web,” and is therefore a hybrid service that qualifies as an online search engine under the DSA.

The Commission’s VLOP/VLOSE register, information updated on Aug. 31, 2026, lists OpenAI Ireland Limited / ChatGPT as a VLOSE with 159.1 million average monthly active users, Digital Services Coordinator Ireland, designation 31.08.2026. Reddit Netherlands B.V. is listed at 57.2 million; Roblox at 46.6 million. The Commission said it has now designated 28 very large online platforms and search engines under the DSA. User counts are as reported by the provider, without prejudice to the Commission’s assessment of the methodology.

After notification, the services have four months — i.e. by January 2027 — to comply with the additional DSA obligations for VLOPs and VLOSEs, including assessing and mitigating systemic risks related to illegal content, minors, users’ physical and mental well-being, fundamental rights, electoral processes and public security. The Commission will supervise in cooperation with Coimisiún na Meán for ChatGPT, and the Dutch Authority for Consumers and Markets for Reddit and Roblox. Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen: the designations mean ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox “will now be held to a higher standard of scrutiny and accountability in the European Union.”

stories.hed: The Price of Intelligence: quality-adjusted AI inference prices
stories.dek: Zhu, Oxford, arXiv 2608.29843. Matched-model −0.10 log pts/yr; quality-adjusted −0.73. 87% of the drop is invisible to agency methods.
stories.action: Package as a measurement/CFO research note, not a vendor price cut. Stick to the paper’s own abstract and results: public panel of 21,024 posted-price observations across 3,208 models and 86 providers (Feb. 2024–Aug. 2026). Matched-model (agency) methods: inference prices fell at 0.10 log points a year; quality-adjusted index fell at 0.73, so 87% of the decline is invisible. Per completed task, the buyer’s price stopped falling (reasoning models raised token consumption faster than token prices fell). Excluding contamination-flagged benchmarks leaves rankings intact at 0.998 yet moves the index by 0.49 log points a year. Do not treat the Menlo Ventures $8.4bn enterprise API spend as an official statistical series — the paper flags it as an illustrative private estimate. List prices, not transaction prices.
grafs: Louis Yiven Zhu (University of Oxford) posted “The Price of Intelligence: A Quality-Adjusted Price Index for AI Services” to the Tuesday arXiv mailing (2608.29843; dated August 30, 2026). The panel assembles 21,024 posted-price observations across 3,208 models and 86 providers and joins them to 4,605 benchmark scores. Measured by the matched-model methods statistical agencies apply to software, inference prices fell at 0.10 log points a year. The quality-adjusted index fell at 0.73, so 87% of the decline is invisible to current methods.

Counted per completed task, the paper says the buyer’s price stopped falling. Reasoning models raised token consumption faster than token prices fell, and the seller’s and buyer’s prices diverged. A pre-registered validity audit is the sharpest result: excluding contamination-flagged benchmarks leaves model rankings intact at 0.998 yet moves the index by 0.49 log points a year. Leaderboard-stability arguments, the author writes, are no defence of economic statistics built on benchmarks.

The indices measure posted list prices on one named channel per provider, not transaction prices, so true declines are faster than measured. Dataset and code are released (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22177190). Treat it as a deflator research note for AI-spend and productivity, not a print on any one lab’s API price.

The Form 8-K filed the same day dates the contract to Aug. 26. As part of the PPA, Fervo’s press release says Google has an option to expand offtake by approximately 600 MW, for a total of nearly 1 GW, by June 2030. The 8-K is more precise and more conditional: the company agreed to offer Google a capacity expansion of approximately 600 MW such that total contracted EGS capacity would be not less than approximately 950 MW, with a guaranteed commercial operation date no later than June 2030, subject to Google’s acceptance and a mutually acceptable definitive agreement. stories.hed: FSB Chair Bailey: frontier AI may rewrite cyber-risk economics
stories.dek: Official G20 letter. Flags AI valuations, private credit, and third-party concentration. Not a rulemaking.
stories.action: Package from the official PDF (dated 28 Aug 2026; published for 31 Aug–1 Sep G20 FMCBG). Quote Bailey on frontier AI altering the speed, scale and economics of cyber risk; bare-metal recovery; concentrated third-party providers; stretched AI-related valuations; private-credit vulnerabilities; leverage interacting with AI–hyperscaler cross-investment. Do not invent a stress scenario or loss estimate — the letter has none. Do not treat CNBC’s ‘disorderly correction’ framing as a Bailey quote of that phrase unless matched to the PDF (‘markets remain vulnerable to a potentially disorderly correction’). Letter is policy warning, not a new FSB standard.
grafs: Financial Stability Board Chair Andrew Bailey, in a letter dated 28 August 2026 and published for the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors meetings on 31 August and 1 September, warned that frontier AI models are “showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities.” For the financial system, he wrote, “the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber risk.”

“Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers,” Bailey wrote. He urged firms to prepare for simultaneous disruption across multiple firms or shared technology dependencies, including the ability to restore critical systems and data from “bare metal,” and said many jurisdictions still lack protocols for safe frontier-model release and deployment.

Outside the AI section, Bailey said markets remain vulnerable to a potentially disorderly correction given fragilities in sovereign debt, vulnerabilities in private credit, and stretched asset valuations — “particularly artificial intelligence-related investments.” He also flagged leverage in equity markets interacting with high valuations and market concentration, “in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers.” The letter is a chair warning, not a new FSB rule or quantified loss scenario.

grafs: Aon plc (NYSE: AON) announced Aug. 31 it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire USI from KKR and other shareholders for a total purchase price of $17.0 billion. The purchase price is $16.7 billion on a net basis, reflecting approximately $278 million of certain tax attributes, and represents approximately 14.5 times on a synergized trailing twelve-month adjusted EBITDA basis, the company said. Official: Aon mediaroom, Aug. 31; Form 8-K (accession 0001193125-26-375328) furnishing the release. The 8-K states the Agreement and Plan of Merger was entered Aug. 30, 2026, for a purchase price of $17 billion in cash, subject to downward adjustments for leakage since June 30, 2026.

USI is described as the tenth-largest U.S. insurance broker, with approximately $3 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,500 team members across nearly 200 U.S. offices. Aon expects approximately $395 million in annual run-rate net adjusted EBITDA impact from identified revenue and cost synergies across the combined middle-market platform, and expects the acquisition to be accretive to adjusted EPS in 2028 and thereafter. Funding is expected from new debt across a range of maturities; Aon says it expects to maintain Baa2 (Moody’s) and A- (S&P) and does not expect to repurchase shares in the near term as it prioritizes debt repayment.

Closing is subject to customary conditions, including regulatory approvals, and is expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. Following close, USI Chairman and CEO Mike Sicard will serve as President of Aon plc and global CEO of Middle Market. Do not invent KKR’s remaining stake, check size, or a USI standalone EBITDA print — the 14.5x multiple is on synergized TTM adjusted EBITDA as stated. Personnel color on Aon’s prior CFO transition is not this story.

stories.hed: Nvidia pauses some AI-cloud revenue-share deals, WSJ says
stories.dek: Spokesperson: the compute-access model is still in place. Antitrust flags. 50% take above a threshold is WSJ sourcing, not a company print.
stories.action: Package the WSJ pause against the July revenue-share/credit-support model and Wednesday’s call (take-or-pay floor; share of neocloud revenue above it; “not making loans”). Do not write that Nvidia killed the program — spokesperson said it is still in place and continues to evolve. Do not treat the 50% threshold as a company print. Do not collapse with the $105B Ohio LPS or the >$500B MOUs. Do not say the pause is the 10-Q’s $36B CSA book. Do not name Sharon AI or Firmus as paused.
grafs: The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter, that Nvidia has paused some deals in a financing initiative that offered credit support to AI cloud companies in exchange for a share of revenue. The company stepped back from the program last week, the Journal said, and could still revamp the initiative or fold it into another program. WSJ exclusive timestamp: Aug. 27, 5:46 p.m. ET. Reuters recaps: CNA and The Straits Times.

An Nvidia spokesperson told Reuters: “The new business model … that opens up compute access to the fast-growing AI ecosystem is still in place and continues to evolve due to high demand.” Do not write that Nvidia killed the program. The 50 percent take above a threshold is the Journal’s account of proposed deals, from people familiar — not a number Nvidia has published.

On Wednesday’s FQ2 call (official IR transcript, FactSet CallStreet), Nvidia described the structure in its own words: a take-or-pay commitment on a portion of a facility’s capacity — “a minimum revenue guarantee that gives lenders the confidence to underwrite the project” — and, in exchange, a share of the neocloud’s revenue earned above that floor. “We’re not making loans.” “In this model, we get paid twice, once on the hardware sale and again through the share of rental revenue,” with “the potential to drive billions in revenue over the medium to long term.” Independent capital still underwrites every deal on its own merits, the company said.

The Journal reported that some Nvidia employees expressed concerns to current and potential customers that the initiative could draw antitrust scrutiny, and that there are sensitivities around how far Nvidia can dictate how customers do business. Nvidia told some cloud providers they could rent its chips out only to approved customers and signaled it preferred capacity be distributed among multiple smaller firms rather than one large customer, the report said. Investor circular-deal scrutiny is the backdrop; do not collapse this pause with the signed $105 billion Ohio LPS cap or the preliminary >$500 billion financing MOUs already on this plate. The July blog named Sharon AI and Firmus as among the first companies on the model — the WSJ recap does not say those specific deals were paused, so do not write that.

grafs: Andreessen Horowitz announced Aug. 28 that it has raised $1.1 billion for a new Machine Age Fund aimed at “the physical buildout of AI.” The official post on a16z.news says the vehicle will invest across computer infrastructure on which AI runs — chips, memory, networking, and storage — plus full systems from data centers to robotics and home AI appliances. The firm frames hardware as an official motion, not a side bet beside its software franchise.

The post argues supply chains are hitting physics and capacity walls as demand jumps: compute density per rack up 28× from an H100 rack to a Rubin rack; rack power from roughly 5–10 kW toward 100–250 kW today and 1 MW over the next three years; data-center scale moving toward hundreds of MW and, in some cases, GW campuses. It says the hardware supply side is used to 20–30% annual growth, “not the triple-digit growth that’s needed.” Signatories named on the post include Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, and David George. Limited partners, cheque sizes, and stage focus were not disclosed.

TechCrunch (6:24 a.m. PDT Aug. 28) confirmed the $1.1 billion raise from the same post. Recent hardware names cited as prior a16z backs — Unconventional AI, Nexthop, Volta, Atoms, Heron Power, Mind Robotics — are examples in the announcement, not reported first closes of Machine Age. Keep this separate from a16z’s January multi-fund raise package.

stories.hed: Your AI, On a Dial
stories.dek: Park et al. arXiv 2608.22852. Tuesday mailing. One MLP neuron steers buy/sell on five open-weight models. Closed models out of scope. Not a product lever.
stories.action: Read as a research note. Forge has no activation access. Do not treat the dial as a product lever.
grafs: Sahong Park and co-authors posted “Your AI, On a Dial: Controlling Investment Bias in LLMs with a Single Neuron” to the Tuesday arXiv mailing (2608.22852; cs.AI, cross-list q-fin). The intervention is one MLP neuron at inference time. It shifts a model-level buy/sell prior without changing the prompt or the weights, and without targeting particular firms. The tests are five open-weight models: Qwen3-8B, Llama-4-Scout, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, Gemma-4-12B-it and Mistral-Small-24B.

Across those five, the dial produces monotonic changes in investment stance. Under identical inputs it also shifts the evidential emphasis of the generated rationales, and in an agentic retrieval setting it changes what the model searches for, which evidence it opens, and what lands in the memo. In long context the dial holds while a matched system-prompt instruction attenuates. An exploratory weekly-news backtest moves rankings and portfolio composition; the authors flag it as not investment alpha.

Closed models are out of scope. The method needs access to internal activations, which we do not have. Forge confirmed there is no activation access here. Treat the paper as a research note, not a product lever.

stories.hed: Do not treat the LLM label as the construct
stories.dek: Dell and Rambachan. arXiv 2608.23524. NBER methods lecture. Rubric, random validation sample, de-bias. Prompt and model search can flip the sign.
stories.action: Do not ship an LLM-labeled series as the construct. Rubric, random validation sample, de-bias. Prompt/model search can flip the sign.
grafs: Melissa Dell and Ashesh Rambachan posted “The Measurement Revolution? Credible Measurement and Inference in the Age of AI” to arXiv (2608.23524), accompanying the NBER 2026 Methods Lecture on estimation and inference with AI-generated data. AI makes it cheap to turn text and images into structured variables. The bottleneck, they argue, is no longer finding any scalable measure of a phenomenon; it is choosing among many that can support different conclusions.

Do not treat LLM labels as the construct. A rubric does not pin down the model, the prompt, or the settings. Ludwig, Mullainathan and Rambachan (2026) document that varying the language model and the prompt can move estimates in magnitude, in statistical significance, and in sign. Baumann and co-authors (2025), replicating 21 published annotation tasks, show that a handful of prompt paraphrases can make virtually any hypothesis appear statistically significant.

The route they defend is validation, not proxy talk: write an explicit rubric, label a random validation sample, and de-bias the downstream estimate. Prediction errors are learned from that design even if the model is arbitrarily biased. Agreement across models is weaker evidence than it looks — frontier systems share architectures and training data. When a random validation sample is unavailable, identification rests on assumptions about how the models err, which have to be stated.

stories.hed: KellyBoost: growth wins the loss, not the book
stories.dek: Li. arXiv 2608.23393. Exact Kelly loss on multi-output XGBoost. Growth beats the classification surrogate. Full-Kelly concentrates and loses to predict-then-optimize.
stories.action: Keep the 2×2: growth beats the surrogate. Do not write full-Kelly as a win over predict-then-optimize. No public GitHub.
grafs: Jiayu Li posted “KellyBoost: Growth-Optimal Portfolio Construction with Gradient-Boosted Trees” to arXiv (2608.23393). End-to-end portfolio learning — map features straight to weights under a financial objective, with no intermediate return forecast — had required backpropagation, which shut out gradient-boosted trees. KellyBoost is a single multi-output XGBoost whose softmax is the portfolio and whose training loss is −log(1 + w⊤y), the exact Kelly growth objective, not a surrogate.

On a 23-year, eight-asset public-data testbed under a separated selection/estimation protocol, a 2×2 of {boosted tree, MLP} × {growth objective, classification surrogate} finds the growth objective improves deployed log growth over the surrogate within both learner classes, in both of two independently built feature pipelines: four of four cells. Because the growth objective also trades less in every cell, transaction costs widen the gap rather than eroding it.

The same testbed prices the boundary. Faithfully optimizing an estimated conditional full-Kelly allocation concentrates aggressively, and in this regime the end-to-end learners trail the classic two-stage predict-then-optimize pipeline, whose squared-error forecasts shrink toward zero and whose optimizer therefore holds milder books. The paper does not list a public GitHub; do not invent one.

stories.hed: Arbitrage-aware latent diffusion for IV surface paths
stories.dek: Buchegger and Gonon, St. Gallen. arXiv 2608.22478. Joint 30-step IVS–return trajectories. Pair with Hashimoto et al. 2608.20842, already on this paper.
stories.action: Pair with 2608.20842: score generators on the compatibility gap, not smile RMSE. Persistence still wins the one-day point forecast.
grafs: Dominik Manuel Buchegger and Lukas Gonon of the University of St. Gallen posted “Arbitrage-Aware Multi-Step Forecasting of Implied Volatility Surfaces” to arXiv (2608.22478). A conditional latent diffusion framework generates joint 30-step trajectories of implied volatility surfaces and underlying returns. An arbitrage-aware autoencoder learns a low-dimensional surface representation; the diffusion model then captures the conditional joint evolution. Admissibility is regularised into the reconstruction map rather than patched on afterwards.

Evaluated on SPX surfaces, the model generates realistic probabilistic multi-step scenarios and also outperforms the persistence benchmark in point forecasting from about weekly horizons onward. Persistence remains superior at one day. The principal limitation is underdispersion: predictive intervals widen with the horizon but stay too narrow. Generated surfaces remain essentially free of static arbitrage.

Read it next to Hashimoto, Hirano, Ozaki and Imajo (2608.20842), already on this paper: the hedging test is whether a strategy trained on synthetic paths still works in the true market, not how well the generator matches stylized facts. A listed GitHub path in the paper did not fetch this morning; the arXiv abstract did.

stories.hed: Lean Marketron: 18 parameters down to 9
stories.dek: Itkin, NYU Tandon. arXiv 2608.20589. Monday q-fin. Gauge-fix the inelastic marketron so flow risk is identifiable.
stories.action: Read the 9-parameter core and the market-price-of-flow-risk wedge. Do not recalibrate the 18.
grafs: Andrey Itkin of NYU Tandon posted “Calibrating Inelastic Markets to Options: The Lean Marketron and the Generalized Langevin Equation” to arXiv (2608.20589) on the q-fin list. The Marketron model and its option-pricing extension suffered from structural non-identifiability: an 18-parameter space trapped solvers in local minima.

By removing exact scaling gauges and sign symmetries, freezing non-financial parameters, and adiabatically eliminating the fast hidden signal, he derives a nine-parameter reduced model. A Gauss-Newton Hessian with empty null space and a manifold-boundary analysis confirm that the reduced core carries no exact symmetry and admits no further reduction.

A staged calibration from the physical measure to the risk-neutral measure, illustrated on SPX options, fits the whole surface with a single parameter set. The wedge between physical and pricing values of the flow block becomes a well-defined market price of flow risk rather than a ridge artifact.

stories.hed: Deep hedging: compatibility, not fidelity
stories.dek: Hashimoto, Hirano, Ozaki, Imajo. arXiv 2608.20842. The gap that matters is whether the strategy still works in the true market.
stories.action: Score generators on the compatibility gap, not stylized-fact RMSE.
grafs: Ryuji Hashimoto, Masanori Hirano, Ryota Ozaki and Kentaro Imajo (University of Tokyo and Preferred Networks) posted “Rethinking Synthetic Scenario Realism: Compatibility, Not Fidelity, Drives Hedging Performance” to arXiv (2608.20842).

Deep hedging trains on synthetic paths because real market data is scarce. The literature scores generators on realism — how well they match stylized facts. The authors define compatibility as whether a strategy trained on the synthetic measure still works in the true market. Hedging performance decomposes into learning error and a compatibility gap; realism and compatibility can diverge.

Empirically, performance is governed by alignment between generator and hedger, plus task structure — path dependence, transaction costs — not by realism alone. Rankings of generators reorder when the hedger class or the option changes.
